description: Soap is not “magic”. It attacks the fatty shell of certain viruses and pulls them out of your skin. Here's why 20 seconds matters.

hero.hook: A simple weapon against viruses: molecules that like water… and fat.

blocks.text: During the COVID-19 pandemic, a very simple gesture has once again become central: washing your hands with soap. No need for a laboratory. Just water, soap, and a little time.
Why does it work so well? Because many dangerous viruses carry an envelope made of fat. And soap is excellent for destroying grease.
Some viruses, such as **coronavirus** or the flu virus, have an outer covering made of lipids (fats). This envelope protects them… until it encounters soap.
Other viruses, called “naked”, do not have this envelope. They are more resistant to soap and alcohol. Fortunately, many of the viruses that travel through hands and droplets are enveloped.

blocks.caption: Rubbing helps the soap reach every corner of the hands.

blocks.text: Soap molecules are . They have a head that likes water and a tail that likes fat. The tail sinks into the fatty envelope of the virus. The head remains turned towards the water. [[surfactants]]
Result: the envelope tears. The virus is disabled. Then the water carries away the debris. Soap does not “burn” the virus like an acid: it **dissolve** and removes it.
It's the same principle that removes grease from a pan: the soap grabs the grease and lets it go with the water.
It takes time for the soap to reach all the folds: between the fingers, under the nails, around the wrists. Around **20 seconds** of friction, this is the minimum often recommended.
Without friction, soap works less well. Water alone either: it does not effectively attack the fatty envelope.

A gel with at least **60%** alcohol can also destroy many enveloped viruses. But if there is visible dirt or grease, the gel is less effective: the dirt acts as a screen. In this case, soap and water remains the best choice.
Soap kills many viruses by tearing away their fatty coverings and then washing them away with the water. Time + friction = efficiency.
